title: Most Americans Retire Earlier Than Planned and Wish They Had Saved More
excerpt: A new TIAA Institute report finds 52% of retirees left the workforce before they expected, with three-quarters regretting they didn't start saving sooner.
body:
• 52% of retirees left the workforce earlier than planned, averaging an age of 57.
  • 76% of retirees wish they had started saving earlier in their careers.
  • The gap between expected and actual retirement age can lead to significant financial consequences.
  • Top reasons for early retirement include health issues, unexpected job loss, and being financially ready sooner than expected.

Most Americans leave the workforce sooner than they expect — and they pay for it in regret. A sweeping new report from the TIAA Institute, released on July 22, finds that 52% of retirees retired earlier than planned, at an average age of just 57. Only 6% retired later than expected.

Meanwhile, workers still on the job expect to retire at 62, according to the survey of 1,591 adults ages 22 to 75. Separate annual surveys from the Employee Benefit Research Institute and the Transamerica Center for Retirement Studies put the expected retirement age even later, at 65 or beyond — with 39% of workers planning to work past 70.

An Expensive Gap Between Plans and Reality

The five-year gap between when retirees actually stopped working and when today's workers expect to has stark financial consequences. Fewer working years means less time to save, less time for investments to compound, and a longer retirement to fund.

"People are expressing regret," said Surya Kolluri, head of TIAA Institute. "That's a powerful emotion. We can take that emotion and apply it to people who have not left the workforce."

"It could be a health incident. It could be caregiving. It could be displacement. It could be AI."

— Surya Kolluri, Head of TIAA Institute

A staggering 76% of retirees wish they had started saving earlier in their careers, and 71% wish they had put away more money. These aren't niche concerns — they are the overwhelming consensus of people who have already crossed the finish line.

Why Retirement Comes Early

The reasons people retire ahead of schedule rarely match what they anticipated. A separate 2026 study from Allianz Life found that 42% of Americans retired earlier than planned, with the top causes being health issues preventing work (30%), unexpected job loss (21%), and being financially ready earlier than expected (21%).

That stands in sharp contrast to what workers still in the workforce envision. Those who haven't yet retired said the most likely reasons they'd leave early would be wanting more time with family (36%), feeling financially ready (32%), and wanting to reduce stress (31%) — aspirational outcomes rather than forced exits.

"When retirement comes early, it can quickly turn a solid plan into a fragile one," said Kelly LaVigne, VP of consumer insights at Allianz Life. "Fewer working years and more retirement years can put significant pressure on savings — especially when early retirement isn't a choice."

Career Disruptions Add Up

The TIAA Institute data shows roughly half of U.S. adults have exited the workforce for more than a year at some point, most commonly to care for children, or due to career changes, burnout, layoffs, or relocation. Each gap reduces lifetime savings and compounds the risk of falling short in retirement.

Roughly eight in ten workers have changed employers at least once, averaging 4.2 moves over a career. A quarter left a job before fully vesting, forfeiting employer matching contributions. These transitions — especially without professional guidance — quietly erode retirement readiness.

The Advisor Advantage

One of the most striking findings in the TIAA research: working with a financial advisor cuts retirement regrets nearly in half. Just 26% of advised retirees regretted underestimating major life events, compared with 43% of those without professional support. Advised retirees were far more likely to describe planning using words like "secure" and "confident."

Yet only 24% of Americans currently work with a financial professional for retirement, tax, or investment planning. Retirees are nearly twice as likely as non-retirees to have an advisor — suggesting many people don't seek help until after it's most needed.

What Workers Can Do Now

Kolluri's advice: plan for multiple retirement scenarios. "Given this data, I would say, let's do three scenarios — 57, 62, and 65," he said. The 401(k) contribution limit in 2026 stands at $24,500, with catch-up contributions pushing the ceiling to $32,500 for workers 50 and older and $35,750 for those aged 60 to 63.

A Stanford University study cited in the report found that delaying retirement by just three to six months has the same impact on savings as raising a 401(k) contribution rate by a full percentage point for 30 years. For those nearing the end of their careers, even a short extension can be transformative.

Starting in 2025, most new 401(k) plans were required to automatically enroll employees — a policy shift that has already lifted participation rates. In the TIAA survey, 70% of workers said their employer offers a retirement plan, 89% of those are enrolled, and three-fifths were auto-enrolled.

The generational shift in retirement funding is already underway. Current retirees leaned most heavily on Social Security and employer pensions; future retirees expect their largest income source to be retirement accounts. Confidence in Social Security tracks with age — 94% of boomers plan to draw on it, compared with just 51% of Gen Z.
image_caption: A growing body of research shows that most Americans retire earlier than planned, often due to health issues or job loss, and wish they had saved more.
nri_angle: Indian Americans planning long careers in the U.S. face the same early-retirement risks; the TIAA data underscores the importance of maximizing 401(k) contributions and planning for retirement scenarios well before age 65.
